## Before the bench {.center}

### What you are about to measure

You have a board that says it has a **16-bit** converter.

By the end of the session you will know:

- how many bits it actually delivers;
- how far off its zero and its scale are, and how well you can correct them;
- whether the samples arrived when the board says they did;
- and whether any of it depends on the computer you plugged it into.

None of those numbers is in a datasheet. All of them are measurable in three
hours with a voltage reference and a multimeter.

### The rule of the session

::: {.callout-important}
## A number without an uncertainty is not a measurement

Everything today ends in an uncertainty budget. Not because the budget is the
point, but because it is the only way to find out which part of the
measurement is worth improving.
:::

## At the bench {.center}

### What you will build

A voltage reference, a divider, and two wires.

::: {.smaller}
| Point | Source | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 0 V | Pin shorted to GND | Offset |
| $\approx V_\mathrm{ref}/2$ | Reference through a divider | The middle of the range |
| $V_\mathrm{ref,IC}$ | Reference IC | Gain |
:::

Plus one long recording with a second channel **shorted to ground** — the
noise floor with no source in it — and the same recording repeated on a second
host.

### Five runs, five sidecars

```bash
arduino-io mode 15 analog
arduino-io stream 15 --hz 1000 --seconds 0.2 --csv data/cal-0v.csv
# ... re-wire, re-measure with the DMM, repeat for 1v25 and 2v50

arduino-io mode 16 analog
arduino-io stream 15,16 --hz 1000 --seconds 5 --csv data/noise-linux.csv
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two things that ruin the session

Measure the DMM reading **at the pin**, every time you re-wire. And copy the
**whole** stream summary line into the sidecar: it is the only evidence that
the recording is complete.
:::

### Then

Open [the handbook](handbook.qmd) for the full procedure, and one of the two
analysis templates — [Python](analysis-py.qmd) or [R](analysis-r.qmd).

They have the same sections and produce the same numbers. Both ship with
reference data, so you can read the whole analysis before you wire anything.

## What you should come away with {.center}

### Three sentences you should be able to defend

1. "This board's converter reports $n$ bits and delivers about $m$ effective
   bits, measured as the spread of $N$ readings of a constant input."
2. "Its sampling grid over five seconds was regular to within
   $\pm x\ \mu$s, with $k$ schedule restarts, and the departure is
   *bounded* / *accumulating* / *stepped*."
3. "The dominant term in the budget is $\dots$, at $h\,\%$ of the variance, and
   the way to reduce it is $\dots$."

If you can say those three with your own numbers in them, the session worked.
